clean_story:
"Existence. Self-sustaining chemistry.
The word 'life' traces to Old English līf, meaning the state of being alive, reflecting its core: a process that maintains and replicates itself.

Life seems simple—eat, grow, reproduce—but its mechanism is a nanoscale factory. A single cell, like E. coli, packs DNA, proteins, and lipids into a space 1000 times thinner than a hair. DNA acts like a recipe book, proteins like workers folding and cutting, lipids like walls keeping it all contained. In the Atacama Desert, some bacteria survive for decades without water, reviving with a single drop. In the deep ocean, tube worms thrive on chemicals from hydrothermal vents, never seeing sunlight. Life adapts by rewriting its own code: CRISPR in bacteria snips viral DNA like molecular scissors, turning invaders into immune memories. Yet all life shares a common ancestor, a microbe from over 3.7 billion years ago, proven by identical genetic sequences in every organism tested so far.
Three related subjects are evolution, cellular respiration and synthetic biology."
